node.label: John Brewer
node.date_label: The Sinews of Power (1989) · Consumption and the World of Goods (coeditor Roy Porter) (1993) · The Pleasures of the Imagination (1997)
node.description: Historian of eighteenth-century Britain whose work crosses state finance, cultural production and consumption. In his2026 memoir Brewer explains that The Sinews of Power challenged the idea of a weak British state while investigating resistance and special interests within fiscal expansion. He resists fixed disciplinary labels and treats literature and the arts as connected historical practices rather than autonomous masterpieces.

incident_edges.relationship: The Sinews of Power makes taxation, administration and the financing of war central to the eighteenth-century British state.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Brewer’s own2026 research retrospective also emphasizes resistance and policy-shaping by interests; strong state does not mean unlimited state.

incident_edges.relationship: The Pleasures of the Imagination examines cultural making and reception across arts and provincial settings.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Peter Holland’s1998 substantial opening on Bewick, John Marsh and cultural interpretation; mediated reading, not complete-book verification.

named_group_routes.relationship: De Vries links household labor and demand; Brewer and Porter collect wider questions about goods and economic life
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. The comparison remains undirected. The new separate contribution records the particular industrious-revolution argument, not a general direction for every overlap. The comparison now includes primary McKendrick, Weatherill and Vickery passages: acceleration, ownership, household work and material meanings are different outcomes, with unequal evidence coverage.

sources.title: Jan de Vries, “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution,” Journal of Economic History 54(2) (June 1994): 249–270.
sources.citation: Jan de Vries, “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution,” Journal of Economic History 54(2) (June 1994): 249–270.

verification.note: University-hosted primary scan downloaded and visually read at pp. 249–252 and 259–264. Supports household labor/resource reallocation, demand, explicit use of historical demography, and qualifications about intrahousehold interests and ideal types. The article criticizes McKendrick’s gendered wording and discusses Sabean’s household critique. No claim that all households followed this trajectory; quantitative estimates and later reception not independently replicated. Addendum 2026-10-18: Pp. 249–251 re-read for revision 1.145 (page images OCRed): the framing against the revision of Lindert and Williamson, Harley and Crafts, and n. 5 citing Berg and Hudson and Cannadine. Addendum 2026-10-18: Revision 1.146 read the publisher abstract and the reference list on Cambridge Core (doi:10.1017/S0022050700014467); the url is the DOI (source_field_sets). The page readings recorded above were made in earlier revisions and were not repeated in 1.146. The new jan_de_vries entry and the revised edge_1085 quote the 1994 article only from its publisher abstract; previously accepted page-based claims remain as accepted.
